text: Most midfielders look at the ball.
Pedri looks at everything else first.
And that one habit is why he almost never loses it.
In the next ten minutes you'll learn three habits that make Pedri look like he has more time than everyone else.
None of them need talent. All of them need practice.
And at the end, I'll give you a ten-minute drill you can do tomorrow with four cones and one friend.
Pedri grew up in Tegueste, a small town in Tenerife, and played for Las Palmas before Barcelona signed him.
He arrived in 2020 as a teenager, and in his first season he played fifty-two times — more than anyone in the squad.
By the end of 2021 he had won the Golden Boy and the Kopa Trophy, the two biggest awards for young players in the world.
He isn't the fastest player on the pitch. He isn't the strongest.
What he does better than almost anyone is decide early. And deciding early is a skill you can copy.
Habit one. Scan before you receive.
Watch the moment the pass leaves the defender's foot. That's roughly a second and a half before the ball reaches the midfielder.
An average player spends that time watching the ball travel.
Pedri spends it looking away from the ball.
First over one shoulder. Where's the nearest opponent?
Then over the other. Where's the free teammate? Where's the space?
By the time the ball arrives, the decision is already made.
Here's the same moment twice.
Without the scan, the player receives, looks up, and only then sees the opponent closing in. Half a second too late.
With the scan, he already knows the pressure is coming from his left. So he takes his first touch to the right — and he's gone.
The rule is simple enough to remember in a match:
Left shoulder. Right shoulder. Then the ball.
Coaches call this scanning, and the best midfielders in the world do it constantly — not once, but every few seconds, even when the ball is far away.
Start with one rule: never receive a pass without having looked away from it at least once.
The most common mistake? Scanning too early.
If you look around, then watch the ball for three seconds, the picture is already out of date.
The best moment for your last look is just as the pass is played — when the ball is travelling and nobody can take it from you.
You can practise this alone. Play the ball against a wall, and every time it leaves your foot, turn your head and name one thing behind you. A tree. A fence. A colour.
It feels silly for a week. Then it becomes automatic.
Habit two. Receive on the half-turn.
Most players receive with their back to the game. Shoulders square to the passer, hips pointing back towards their own goal.
From there, the only easy pass is the one that goes backwards.
Now open the body. Not all the way — about halfway, so you can still see the passer and the pitch in front of you at the same time.
Look at what changes. Back, sideways, forward. Three options instead of one.
The trick is in the feet. Pedri lets the ball run across his body and takes it with the foot furthest from the pass.
That one detail turns him the moment he touches it. No extra touch. No wasted second.
If habit one tells you where to go, habit two lets you get there in one touch.
Watch out for the opposite mistake: opening up so much that you turn your back on the passer.
Now a heavy pass or a bad bounce catches you off guard, and the ball runs away from you.
Halfway is the sweet spot. You see the ball, you see the pitch, and your hips are already pointing where you want to go.
To practise it, put a cone two metres to your side. Every pass you receive, your first touch has to go past that cone — never back towards the wall.
Habit three is the one you won't find on a stats sheet.
Make the next pass easy.
A pass isn't finished when it arrives. It's finished when your teammate can do something with it.
Watch this: the first pass is technically perfect — but it goes to his weaker foot, slowly, with an opponent closing. He survives, but only just.
Now the same pass, played to his far foot, a little firmer, a little earlier. He doesn't even need to control it.
That's what Pedri's teammates mean when they say playing with him is easy. He isn't just passing the ball. He's passing time.
So before you pass, ask one question: which foot, and how fast?
The foot is usually the one furthest from the nearest opponent.
The speed depends on the pressure. If your teammate is free, a soft pass gives him time to look up. If he's marked, a firmer pass gets there before the defender does.
Notice that you can only make that choice if you scanned first. The three habits aren't separate tricks. They're one chain:
See early. Turn in one touch. Give your teammate an easier ball than the one you received.
Here's the drill. Four cones in a ten-metre square — four different colours.
You stand in the middle. A friend passes to you from outside the square.
Just before each pass, they point at one cone behind you. You have to scan, find it, receive on the half-turn, and play out through that side.
Three minutes slow. Three minutes at match speed. Three minutes with one touch only.
Ten minutes, three habits, every time you train.
